node.label: Erika Lee
node.date_label: At America’s Gates (2003) · Angel Island, with Judy Yung (2010) · The Making of Asian America (2015) · America for Americans (2019)
node.description: In At America’s Gates (2003), Erika Lee argued that Chinese exclusion helped make the United States a gatekeeping nation. Immigration restrictions reshaped Chinese American lives while expanding federal identification, surveillance, border enforcement and deportation. The book received the Theodore Saloutos Memorial Book Award and the Association for Asian American Studies History Book Award. America for Americans (2019) treats xenophobia as an enduring American tradition. Reviewing that book, Fred H. Lawson questioned whether its episodic structure establishes continuity and whether it adequately distinguishes racial hostility from religious prejudice and other forms of exclusion.

proposed_edges.relationship: Lee’s 2006 “A Nation of Immigrants and a Gatekeeping Nation” uses Ngai’s Impossible Subjects (2004) to explain racialized nationality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 13: “As Mae Ngai has shown”; cites Ngai p. 27. Ngai’s book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Lee’s 2006 “A Nation of Immigrants and a Gatekeeping Nation” uses Jacobson’s Whiteness of a Different Color (1998) on consolidated whiteness.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 13: “Jacobson further explains”; cites Jacobson p. 14. Jacobson’s book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Lee’s 2006 “A Nation of Immigrants and a Gatekeeping Nation” uses Gabaccia’s From the Other Side (1994) on gendered exclusion.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 11: “As Donna Gabaccia explains”; cites Gabaccia p. 37. Gabaccia’s book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “A Nation of Immigrants and a Gatekeeping Nation” (2006), Lee sets the argument that Chinese exclusion made the United States a gatekeeping nation against earlier historians, citing Higham’s Strangers in the Land (1955; cited in the 1978 edition), who treated anti-Asian movements as “historically tangential” to American nativism and the 1920s as the decisive period of restriction.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Manuscript p. 9, paragraph beginning “Some of our leading scholars,” and note 19, p. 28, explicitly identify Higham. Short phrase: “historically tangential.” Published text not read beyond extract; Higham unread. The critique concerns narrative placement, not his whole scholarship.

proposed_edges.relationship: According to its abstract, “The ‘Yellow Peril’ and Asian Exclusion in the Americas” (2007) examines Asian migration and exclusion across North and South America and the transnational nature of anti-Asian racism, as a contribution to the global history of race.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 537–538, 556–557: “hemispheric Orientalism.” Selected passages only; comparative national distinctions retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “A Nation of Immigrants and a Gatekeeping Nation” (2006), Lee uses Omi and Winant’s concept of racial formation to describe how late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century immigration debates and policies produced new understandings and definitions of race and racial categories.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 545 and conclusion p. 557: “I build upon Winant’s claim.” Winant’s book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Lee led the original #ImmigrationSyllabus (2017), a collaborative resource explaining immigration history for teachers, students and the public.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 2017 Libraries article, opening description and organizers; current About page, original-project credits. Later 2026 revision has separate leadership.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘America First, Immigrants Last: American Xenophobia Then and Now’ (delivered 2018; published 2019–20), Erika Lee argued for a more expansive definition of xenophobia as a constant, adaptable force in U.S. history, against the view that it peaked in the Gilded Age and Progressive Era and receded after the 1965 Immigration Act.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete editorial on Cambridge Core. Genetin-Pilawa and Cothran identify Lee’s intervention in the periodization and definition of xenophobia, including her challenge to the interpretation of 1965 as a turning point away from exclusion. Also read Lee’s publisher abstract and publication metadata: the abstract explicitly connects xenophobia with progressive reform and the expansion of state capacity. Her article body remains unread. This is a field contribution supported by the editorial and abstract, not a claim that the editors adopted Lee’s framework in their own research. Mapping to political history is an editorial classification of the specified argument about policy and power.

proposed_edges.relationship: Through Immigrant Stories (launched in 2013), Erika Lee helped connect immigration history with digital humanities by developing a collaborative project that lets immigrants and refugees create digital accounts of migration for archival preservation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the Radcliffe institutional profile and the IHRC’s project account. The profile names Lee’s role in launching Immigrant Stories and describes its multilingual storytelling website. The project account supplies the original 2013 launch date, participant control over the form and content of stories, video creation, and preservation and discovery through library collections. Credit remains collaborative: the IHRC launched the project, and Lee is not represented as its sole creator or software developer. This edge records digital creation and preservation of historical evidence; the input already records her public-history contribution. No individual participant narrative was opened or quoted.
